extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers writing academic research reports (undergraduate and graduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for revising organization, argument, citations, abstracts, and visual presentation in academic research reports; includes rules for citation styles, paragraph/section structure, and designing tables/charts/graphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a consistent citation style and consult its guide
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be easier if we all cited sources in the same style, but we don't. For academic research, there are two basic patterns, each with two common versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find out which style you should use and consult the proper guide for your style (or a reliable online guide). Many researchers use citation software, but some teachers expect students not to rely on it—ask your instructor. Follow the style guide's prescriptions down to the last comma, space, and capital letter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two basic citation patterns: author-title and author-date
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation styles are distinguished by what follows the author: if the title follows the author, it's author-title; if the date follows the author, it's author-date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author-title is common in the humanities (emphasizes the work itself); author-date is used in natural and social sciences (readers want to see how old a source is). Format examples: Author-Title: Anes, Lee f. A Story of Ohio: Its Early Days. Boston: Hobson Press, 1988. Author-Date: Anes, Lee. 1988. A story of Ohio: Its early days. Boston: Hobson Press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-title common variants (Chicago/Turabian and MLA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two versions of author-title style are Chicago (The Chicago Manual of Style / Turabian) and MLA (MLA Handbook for Writers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These styles differ in minor details but those details matter—consult the specific manual for exact forms and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-date common variants (Chicago/Turabian and APA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two versions of author-date style are Chicago (also sometimes called Turabian) and APA (Publication Manual of the American Psychological Association).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Again, differences are minor but important—consult the appropriate guide and obey its punctuation, spacing, and capitalization rules exactly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate citations wherever you use a source
rubrics_metrics.description: You must indicate in your text every place where you use a source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parenthetical citations are the most common method across the four major styles: include enough information to find the corresponding entry in the list of sources and specific page numbers when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parenthetical citation formats and rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A parenthetical citation includes only the information a reader needs to find the source in your list of sources. What you include depends on author-title vs author-date style and on the style manual (Chicago, MLA, APA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Author, page(s) — (Author, 220). MLA: (Author 220). If you list more than one publication by the same author, add a short title: (Author, Short Title, page[s]). In author-date style add the date: (Author date, page[s]) or APA: (Author, date, p. xxx). If you have mentioned the author in sentence, drop the name from the parenthetical citation and include only the relevant elements (e.g., page or date+page). For further rules (multiple authors, multiple works), consult the specific style guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chicago author-title notes vs bibliography forms
rubrics_metrics.description: In Chicago author-title style you may use raised numbers directing readers to notes, which include the same information as a bibliography entry but differ in form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes list names as first name last name, separate elements with commas rather than periods, and put publication data in parentheses. Example note: 5. George Smith, Travels in Cuba (Boston: Hasbro Press, 1999), 233. Bibliography form: Smith, George. Travels in Cuba. Boston: Hasbro Press, 1999.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think like a reader when revising (top-down revision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers want a sense of the whole, its structure, and why they should read your report; they then use that sense to interpret the parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start revising overall organization first, then sections, then sentences, and last matters of spelling and punctuation. Systematic top-down revision helps you read your draft the way a reader will rather than reading into what you want.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise the frame: make introduction, conclusion, and main point clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers must recognize three things instantly and unambiguously: where your introduction stops, where your conclusion begins, and what sentence states your main point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Put extra space after your introduction and before your conclusion; if permitted, use headings at those joints. 2) State your main point at or near the end of the introduction and compare it with the conclusion's point so they do not contradict—make the conclusion more specific and contestable. 3) If your introduction's point is only a launching point, revise it to add the key concepts that run through the report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the substance of your argument (structure match and evidence check)
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the structure of your argument matches the structure of your report and identify evidence within each section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Ensure each reason is the point of its own section; otherwise organization may conflict with argument. 2) In each section, identify everything that counts as evidence (summaries, paraphrases, quotations, facts, figures, graphs, tables). If evidence and its explanation are less than about a third of a section, you may not have enough evidence; if lots of evidence but few reasons, you may have a data dump.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the quality of your argument (sufficiency, hedging, alternatives, warrants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine what might cause readers to reject your argument by checking evidence, qualifications, tone toward readers, and unstated warrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: i) Is evidence sufficient, reliable, and clearly connected to claims? Check data/quotations against notes, show how they relate to claims, and avoid skipping subreasons. ii) Appropriately qualify claims with hedges like probably, may, most. iii) Avoid treating readers as opponents—write as a conversation and acknowledge alternative views or objections. iv) Identify unstated warrants in each section's margin and decide whether readers will accept them; if not, state and support them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise organization: ensure coherence across the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers should find the whole report coherent; use checks to ensure sections and terms unify the report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checklist includes: key terms should run through the whole report (circle key terms in introduction/conclusion and body), beginnings of sections should be signaled, each section's relationship to the previous should be made clear with linking phrases, each section should clearly relate to the whole (answer one of five argument questions or provide context), and the point of each section should be stated in a brief intro or summarize at the end if long.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make section-specific key terms distinctive
rubrics_metrics.description: Each major section needs its own key terms to unify and distinguish it from other sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a heading that uniquely distinguishes the section; find the point sentence and circle its key terms; check that those terms run through the section and differ from the main-point terms. If two sections share identical key terms, consider combining them; if a section lacks unique terms, readers may not see its new contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signal section boundaries and logic clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginnings of each section and subsection must be clearly signaled so readers recognize organization and order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use headings where accepted or add extra space at major joints. Start sections with words that signal how they relate to the previous one (e.g., More important..., The other side of this issue is..., One complication is..., First, Second...). If you can't insert headings confidently, readers likely won't recognize your organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph-level checks: each paragraph must serve its section's point
rubrics_metrics.description: Every paragraph should be relevant to the point of its section and should have an opening sentence that states its point (or put the point in the last sentence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order sentences by principle and keep paragraphs to sensible lengths: avoid very long paragraphs (more than a page in most fields) and avoid long strings of extremely short ones (fewer than five lines). Reserve two- or three-sentence paragraphs mostly for lists, transitions, section intros/conclusions, or emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let drafts cool and perform a paraphrase test
rubrics_metrics.description: After letting your revised draft cool, skim its top-level parts and paraphrase the paper to test coherence and whether the argument hangs together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skim the introduction, first paragraph of major sections, and the conclusion; paraphrase from memory or ask someone else to skim and summarize. The quality of a test reader's summary predicts how well final readers will understand your argument. Revise in light of teacher/adviser feedback—consider each suggestion carefully even if you don't follow all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstracts: purpose and core elements
rubrics_metrics.description: An abstract should be shorter than an introduction but do three things an introduction does: state the research problem, announce key themes, and state the main point or a launching point that anticipates the main point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstracts differ by field but commonly follow one of three patterns: (1) Context + Problem + Main Point (abbreviated introduction with result); (2) Context + Problem + Launching Point (states only the general nature of results); (3) Summary (states context and problem, then summarizes the rest of the report focusing on evidence or procedures). Put likely search keywords in your title and the first sentence of your abstract to help future researchers find your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose visual vs verbal representations based on data complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: When data are few and simple, readers can grasp them in a sentence; if you present more than a few numbers, readers will struggle and need graphics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If numbers are simple (a couple of figures), use a sentence; if more numerous or complex, choose tables, bar charts, or line graphs depending on rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the most effective graphic for the rhetorical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables, bar charts, and line graphs each have distinctive rhetorical effects: tables emphasize precision and discrete numbers; bar charts emphasize contrasts among discrete items; line graphs suggest continuous change over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the form that achieves the effect you want, not the first one that comes to mind. New researchers should limit choices to basic tables, bar charts, and line graphs; advanced researchers may use more specialized graphics appropriate to their field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame each graphic to help readers understand it
rubrics_metrics.description: A graphic representing complex numbers rarely speaks for itself; you must frame it to show readers what to see and how it supports your argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Label every graphic descriptively: table titles flush left above, figure legends flush left below. Keep labels short but descriptive enough to distinguish graphics; avoid general topics and avoid interpretation in the title. 2) Insert into the graphic information that helps readers see how data support your point (e.g., final column showing change, annotations explaining anomalies). 3) Introduce the table/figure with a sentence explaining how to interpret it and highlight the number or relationship you want readers to focus on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep all graphics as simple as their content allows
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers want to see only data relevant to your point, free of distractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include only relevant data (put extra data in appendices), avoid fancy visual effects from software defaults, box graphics only to group multiple figures, do not color or shade backgrounds, and avoid iconic bars or unnecessary 3-D effects. Use color only if printed in color and not likely to be photocopied in black-and-white.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific table design rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize tables so readers can quickly find the point and avoid dense clutter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order rows and columns by a helpful principle (not automatically alphabetic); round numbers to relevant precision; sum totals at the bottom of a column or at the end of a row (not at the top/left); for many-row tables, lightly shade every fifth row or use light gray lines only if needed to direct the eye.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific bar chart rules (grouping and stacked bars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bar charts communicate visually as much as numerically; arrangement of bars should support your message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group and order bars to create an image that matches your message (avoid alphabetical order if it obscures the point). Use stacked bars only when you want readers to compare whole values (not proportions), arrange segments logically (largest at bottom with darkest shade if possible), label segments with specific numbers, and connect corresponding segments across bars with gray lines to assist comparisons. Alternatively, give each part its own bar grouped into clusters when comparing parts across categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chart/graph technical and labeling rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Make charts and graphs readable and precise when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use background grid lines only if the graphic is complex or precise numbers are important; make them light gray. Label both axes; use tick marks and labels to indicate intervals on the vertical axis. When possible, label lines or bar segments directly on the image rather than relying on a separate legend; use a legend only when labels would make the image too complex. When specific numbers matter, add them to bars or to points on lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misleading or decorative visual choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Decorative choices can distort how readers judge values and look amateurish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never use iconic bars (images representing the item) or add a third dimension merely for effect. Plot data in three dimensions only when readers are familiar with such graphs and you cannot present the data otherwise.
